title: Binary Search
tagline: O(log n) on any sorted (or monotonic) space — and the universal template that survives every off-by-one trap.
intro:
Binary search repeatedly halves the search space, finding an answer in O(log n) instead of O(n). Its real power isn't just searching sorted arrays — it's searching any **monotonic** space, where a yes/no condition flips exactly once from false to true. That insight ("binary search on the answer") turns many hard optimisation problems into easy ones.

The reason binary search has a reputation for being tricky is the off-by-one minefield: `lo <= hi` vs `lo < hi`, `mid+1` vs `mid`, infinite loops. The cure is to stop memorising five variants and instead learn **one template** built around the question "find the first index where a condition becomes true". Every variant — exact match, lower bound, rotated array, search-on-answer — is that one template with a different condition.

This module gives you that universal template, the monotonic-predicate mental model, and the rotated-array and search-on-answer variants.
objectives: Recognise sorted OR monotonic-predicate problems as binary-search candidates
Write the universal 'first true' template without off-by-one bugs
Compute mid safely to avoid integer overflow
Find lower/upper bounds (first/last occurrence) of a value
Search a rotated sorted array by deciding which half is sorted
Apply 'binary search on the answer' to min/max feasibility problems

signals: Sorted array + 'find / find first / find last / insert position'
"Minimum/maximum value such that <condition> holds" → search on answer
A monotonic predicate: once true, always true (or vice versa)
O(n) is too slow and the space has order you can exploit
antiSignals: Unsorted data with no monotonic property → sort first or hash
You need all matches, not a boundary → linear scan after finding one
Tiny n where O(n) is already trivial

sections.heading: The big idea in plain words
sections.body:
Binary search is the 'guess my number between 1 and 100' game played perfectly. You guess 50; if you're told 'higher', you instantly forget 1 through 50 and only think about 51 through 100. Every guess throws away half of what's left, so even a million numbers take only about 20 guesses.

Example: find 7 in `[1, 3, 5, 7, 9]`. The middle value is 5, which is smaller than 7, so ignore the whole left half. The middle of what remains is 7 - found in just two checks instead of scanning all five. The catch: this only works when the data is sorted (or otherwise ordered), because that order is what lets you trust 'go this way'.

sections.heading: The mental model: monotonic predicates
sections.body:
Forget 'sorted array' for a moment. Binary search works on any boolean predicate `f(x)` that is **monotonic**: false, false, ..., false, true, true, ..., true. Binary search finds the boundary — the first x where `f(x)` is true.

| Concept | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Search space** | The range `[lo, hi]` of candidate answers |
| **Predicate f(x)** | A yes/no test that flips exactly once |
| **Boundary** | The first x where f(x) becomes true — the answer |
| **Invariant** | f(lo-1) is false, f(hi+1) is true (the answer is in [lo,hi]) |

Searching a sorted array for `target` is just the predicate `f(i) = (arr[i] >= target)`. Reframing every problem as 'find the boundary of a monotonic predicate' is what makes the off-by-ones disappear.

sections.heading: The universal template
sections.body: Use the half-open `[lo, hi)` form. It converges to the first index where the condition holds, and it can't infinite-loop because the range strictly shrinks every iteration.

callouts.text: Compute mid as `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`, not `(lo + hi) / 2`, in Java/C++ to avoid integer overflow when lo and hi are large. Python ints are unbounded so it doesn't matter there.

sections.heading: Exact match, lower bound, upper bound
sections.body:
All three are the universal template with a different predicate.

| Goal | Predicate condition(mid) | After loop |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First index ≥ target (lower bound) | `arr[mid] >= target` | `lo` is insertion point |
| First index > target (upper bound) | `arr[mid] > target` | `lo` is past last match |
| Exact match | lower bound, then check `arr[lo] == target` | found / not found |
| Count of target | `upperBound - lowerBound` | the count |

This is why you only need one template: change the comparison, get a different boundary. First-and-last-position problems are just lower bound and upper bound back to back.

sections.heading: Searching a rotated sorted array
sections.body: A rotated sorted array (e.g. `[4,5,6,7,0,1,2]`) isn't globally sorted, but at any `mid`, **one half is always sorted**. Detect which half is sorted by comparing `arr[lo]` to `arr[mid]`; if `target` lies within that sorted half's range, search it, otherwise search the other half. Still O(log n).

sections.heading: Binary search on the answer
sections.body:
The advanced superpower. When a problem asks for the *minimum (or maximum) value such that some condition is feasible*, and feasibility is monotonic in that value, binary-search the answer itself.

Examples: 'minimum eating speed to finish bananas in h hours' (Koko), 'smallest divisor given a threshold', 'capacity to ship packages in d days', 'split array into k parts minimising the largest sum'. The recipe: define `feasible(x)` (can we do it with value x?), confirm it's monotonic, then binary search the smallest feasible x.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Min value x making it feasible?"] --> B{"feasible(mid)?"}
  B -- Yes --> C["try smaller: hi = mid"]
  B -- No --> D["need bigger: lo = mid + 1"]
  C --> E["converge to smallest feasible x"]
  D --> E
```

callouts.text: The search space here is the range of possible answers (e.g. 1..maxValue), not array indices. The 'array' is conceptual — you evaluate feasible(mid) instead of reading arr[mid].

interviewTalking: Frame it as a boundary search: "The array is sorted, so I can binary search in O(log n). I'll look for the first index where arr[i] >= target using the half-open template, which avoids off-by-one bugs." For optimisation problems, say the magic words: "The feasibility is monotonic — if speed x works, any larger speed works — so I'll binary search on the answer instead of the array." Always mention overflow-safe mid and state O(log n) time, O(1) space.
commonMistakes: Computing mid as (lo + hi) / 2 and overflowing in Java/C++ — use lo + (hi - lo) / 2
Mixing `lo <= hi` (closed) with `hi = mid` (half-open) updates → infinite loop
Updating `lo = mid` instead of `lo = mid + 1`, never shrinking the range
Binary-searching data that isn't sorted or monotonic
In rotated search, comparing to the wrong endpoint to decide which half is sorted
Forgetting to verify arr[lo] == target after a lower-bound search
complexityNotes: Binary search is O(log n) time and O(1) space (iterative). 'Binary search on the answer' is O(log(range) × cost-of-feasibility-check); if each feasibility check is O(n), the total is O(n log(range)).
